results.summary: This design is a chip selector for Ben Eater's breadboard 6502 computer. It takes the high address bits and clock, and generates active-low or active-high chip select signals for ROM, RAM, VIA, UART, and SID. It is intended to be used with the actual breadboard computer or with an LED bar graph for testing. The design is a simple combinational decoder with no internal state, and its behavior is documented with a truth table.

This is a 4-bit carry look-ahead adder implemented in Verilog. It takes two 4-bit operands and a carry input, and produces a 4-bit sum and a carry output. The design is purely combinational and can be used as a building block for larger adders. It was tested on an FPGA, and no external hardware is required.

This project implements an 8-bit function generator targeting the AD5330 parallel DAC. It includes a write-only register interface to select a constant signal, a sine wave, or programmable trapezoid/pulse waveforms with adjustable amplitude, offset, phase, and timing. The design is controlled via input pins and provides DAC control signals and 8-bit data outputs. The documentation is minimal, providing only the pin list and a one-line description, so detailed operation and testing are not described.

Jsilicon is a dual-mode 8-bit CPU/ALU core with manual and automatic (ROM) modes. In manual mode, it acts as an ALU controlled by external opcode and operand inputs, with results shown on output pins and transmitted via UART. In CPU mode, it executes a built-in program from ROM, streaming results to outputs and UART. The design includes a UART transmitter and is intended for educational or embedded use.

This project is a two-player scoreboard controlled by two pushbuttons. It counts points for each player, with short presses incrementing and long presses decrementing the score. The scores are displayed on two 7-segment displays that alternate between showing 'P1' or 'P2' and the respective score. The design includes debounce logic and was tested with testbenches.

This is a digital traffic light controller with pedestrian request handling and MAX7219 display interface. It controls car and pedestrian lights with precise timing, button debouncing, and a countdown displayed on LED matrices. The design includes an FSM, clock divider, MAX7219 driver, and SPI master, and was validated in simulation and Wokwi. It requires external LEDs, pushbuttons, and MAX7219 modules.

This is an analog bandgap voltage reference based on a Beta amplifier topology with a folded cascode OTA. It provides a typical output voltage of approximately 1.23 V. The circuit includes a buffer for one output node and requires an external DC voltage source for testing. Silicon measurements showed a Vref of 1.26 V, close to the expected value.

This project contains two identical 11-stage ring oscillator voltage-controlled oscillators. Each oscillator uses current-starved inverters controlled by an external voltage and a reset input to start or stop oscillation. Silicon tests showed both oscillators working, starting at around 45 mV input. External hardware includes a voltage source and oscilloscope.

This design is a PWM generator that produces a pulse-width modulated signal with a duty cycle resolution of 12.5%. It uses a 5-bit counter and a comparator, with the duty cycle selected by a 3-bit speed input. The output frequency is the clock frequency divided by 32. It requires external pull-down resistors, switches, and an oscilloscope for testing.

This project is an 8-bit pseudo-softmax accelerator for neural networks, implementing a reduced softmax activation function. It takes 8-bit data inputs and produces 8-bit outputs, with selection signals for configuration. The design was tested by comparing the post-synthesis netlist with the RTL using random inputs, but no external hardware is required. The documentation notes that behavioral testing is complex due to the nature of softmax inputs.
